nameStory: The forked fungus beetle gets its name from the distinctive horn-like projections on the male's head that fork into two points, resembling tiny antlers. The 'fungus' part of the name comes from its complete dependence on bracket fungi throughout its entire life cycle. From egg to adult, this beetle lives, feeds, and reproduces exclusively on the tough, shelf-like fungi growing on dead trees.
description: The forked fungus beetle is a small, dark brown to black beetle that spends its entire life on bracket fungi growing from dead trees. Males are easily recognized by their characteristic forked horn projections on their head, while females lack these dramatic features. These sturdy little beetles are typically about 6-12mm long with a somewhat flattened, oval body that's well-suited for living under and within fungal shelves. As members of the darkling beetle family, they have a tough, armor-like appearance.

idTips.label: Male's forked horns
idTips.description: Males have distinctive Y-shaped horn projections extending forward from their head that feel hard and smooth to the touch - females completely lack these structures

idTips.label: Fungal habitat
idTips.description: Always found on or near large bracket fungi on dead trees, particularly the hard, woody shelf fungi with white undersides

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Deep brown to black body with a matte finish that feels rough and grainy, like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: Oval, somewhat flattened profile that allows them to squeeze between fungal layers - feels solid and armored when handled

idTips.label: Size and movement
idTips.description: Small beetles about the size of a fingernail that move slowly and deliberately, often playing dead when disturbed

habitat: Look for forked fungus beetles in mature forests with plenty of dead and dying hardwood trees, particularly where large bracket fungi are growing. They're especially common on Ganoderma fungi - those thick, woody shelf fungi with shiny, varnish-like tops and white undersides that grow from oak, maple, birch, and other deciduous trees. You'll find them from sea level to mid-elevations throughout New England's mixed and deciduous woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots within fungal brackets. Look for mating pairs on fungal surfaces during mild spring days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible on fungal surfaces, feeding and reproducing. This is the best time to spot the distinctive horned males.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active on warm days, preparing for winter by burrowing deeper into their fungal homes. Late fall is good for finding them as they become less active.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate within the fungal brackets, tunneled deep into the tough fungal tissue where they're protected from freezing temperatures.

funFact: This beetle's entire family tree - eggs, larvae, pupae, and adults - never leaves their fungal apartment building, with multiple generations of beetles living together in the same bracket fungus like a multi-generational household that can persist for years!
confusionNotes: Other small dark beetles might be found near fungi, but only male forked fungus beetles have those distinctive Y-shaped horns on their heads. Remember: 'Forked horns, fungus home' - if you see the horns and they're on a bracket fungus, you've found your beetle.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'darkling beetles,' many species in this family are active during the day. The family name Tenebrionidae comes from the Latin 'tenebrio' meaning 'seeker of dark places,' which is more about their preference for hiding in crevices than being strictly nocturnal.
compareHints: The forked fungus beetle is the only species in its genus Bolitotherus in North America, making it unique among darkling beetles for its exclusive relationship with bracket fungi. Other darkling beetles in New England are typically ground-dwelling scavengers found under logs or stones, while this species is exclusively arboreal and fungus-dependent. The male's forked horns are completely unique among New England's darkling beetle species.
